etymology: From Presbyterian (Greek presbyteros, elder) + Scotland; the church order recovered in the Scottish Reformation of 1560 under John Knox, governed by elders in graded courts rather than by bishops or pope.
biblical_def: Scottish Presbyterianism names the Reformed church order that took root in Scotland when, in 1560, the Estates abolished the Mass and the pope's jurisdiction and received the Scots Confession drafted by John Knox and his fellows. Knox, forged in the fires of the French galleys and the Geneva of Calvin, brought home a church governed not by prelates but by elders — kirk session, presbytery, synod, and General Assembly — on the conviction that Christ alone is King and Head of His church and has given her officers in His Word. Andrew Melville pressed the crown-defying claim that there are "two kingdoms" and "twa kings," Christ and the magistrate, each in his own sphere. The National Covenant of 1638 and the Solemn League and Covenant of 1643 bound the nation to that confession; the Westminster Assembly, with its Scottish commissioners, gave Presbyterianism its mature confession and catechisms. The Covenanters of the "Killing Time" sealed it with blood on the moors. This dictionary, confessing the 1689 Baptist standard, honors Scottish Presbyterianism as its nearest kin in doctrine and its elder in suffering, differing only where the Word leads it — on the subjects of baptism and the independency of the congregation — while gladly owning the same sovereign grace.
webster_summary: The Reformed, elder-governed church order recovered in Scotland in 1560 under John Knox; confessed in the Scots Confession and later the Westminster standards; defended by the Covenanters unto death. Honored here as the nearest Reformed kin of the 1689 Baptist confession.
webster_full: SCOTTISH PRESBYTERIANISM, noun. The Reformed faith and church-government established in Scotland at the Reformation of 1560.
Government is by elders in graded courts — session, presbytery, synod, General Assembly — under Christ as sole King and Head of the church.
Doctrinal standards: the Scots Confession (1560), then the Westminster Confession and Catechisms (1646–48).
Defended through the National Covenant (1638), the Solemn League and Covenant (1643), and the blood of the Covenanters in the Killing Time.
Honored by this Baptist dictionary as nearest kin in grace, differing on baptism and congregational independency.
scriptures: And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee.
And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church.
corruption_summary: The danger is not in the doctrine but in the modern drift of the kirk that bore it: the Church of Scotland and its daughters have, in much of their visible body, traded Knox's gospel for liberal theology, women's ordination, and the affirming of what Scripture condemns — a warning that no confession preserves a church that lets go of the Word.
corruption_paragraphs: The historic corruption Scottish Presbyterianism resisted was Rome's — the Mass, the papal supremacy, and the prelacy the Stuart kings tried to force upon the kirk. That battle was won at fearful cost. The modern corruption is subtler and comes from within: large parts of the establishment that Knox founded have embraced higher-critical denials of Scripture, ordained women to the eldership the apostle reserves to qualified men, and blessed unions the Word forbids. A confession framed and gold on the page saves no church whose pulpits no longer believe it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of its history, but it does face the temptation to read the present apostasy back as though it were always there. The principle to recover is the Covenanters' own: Christ alone is King in His church, His Word alone binds the conscience, and a confession is honored only where it is believed and obeyed. The faithful remnant in the free and confessing Presbyterian bodies keeps that flame; this dictionary owns them as brethren.
roots_summary: From Greek presbyteros (elder) — the New Testament office of the elder (also called bishop and pastor), here organized into graded courts; rooted in the Scottish Reformation of 1560.
roots_lines: Greek presbyteros (elder), the New Testament office of oversight (Acts 20:17, 28)
Government by graded assemblies of elders, not by single bishops (presbytery, Acts 15)
Historical root: the Scottish Reformation of 1560 under John Knox
Confessional root: the Scots Confession, then the Westminster standards
Covenantal root: the National Covenant (1638) and Solemn League and Covenant (1643)
usage: Scottish Presbyterianism gave the English-speaking world the Westminster Confession and the metrical Psalms.
The Covenanters of Scottish Presbyterianism died on the moors rather than yield Christ's crown to the king.
This Baptist dictionary calls Scottish Presbyterianism its nearest kin, parting only on baptism and church independency.

etymology: From England + Reformation (Latin reformare, to form anew); the sixteenth-century breaking of the English church from Rome and its gradual reform by the Word of God.
biblical_def: The English Reformation is the sixteenth-century recovery of the gospel in England, begun in tangled motives and brought to fruition by faithful men and the blood of martyrs. It opened with Henry VIII's self-serving breach with Rome over his marriage — a political act, not a converted heart — yet God overruled a king's sin for the freeing of His Word. William Tyndale had already given England the Scriptures in her own tongue and was strangled and burned for it, praying that the Lord would open the king of England's eyes. Under Edward VI, Thomas Cranmer gave the church the Book of Common Prayer and the Forty-Two Articles, planting a Reformed liturgy and confession. Mary Tudor's reign drove the work back in fire: Cranmer, Latimer, and Ridley were burned at Oxford, Latimer bidding Ridley "play the man" and light such a candle as should never be put out. Under Elizabeth the settlement held, and the Thirty-Nine Articles fixed a Reformed doctrine within an episcopal frame. From this soil sprang the Puritans, who judged the Reformation half-finished and pressed for a purer church — and from the Puritans, in time, the Baptists whose confession this dictionary owns.
webster_summary: The sixteenth-century recovery of the gospel in England — begun in Henry VIII's political breach with Rome, advanced by Tyndale's Bible and Cranmer's Prayer Book, sealed by the Oxford martyrs under Mary, and settled in the Thirty-Nine Articles. From its Puritan fruit sprang the Baptists.
webster_full: ENGLISH REFORMATION, noun. The reforming of the church in England in the sixteenth century by the recovery of Scripture and the gospel.
Begun politically in Henry VIII's breach with Rome (1534), but rooted spiritually in Tyndale's English Bible.
Advanced under Edward VI by Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer and the Articles of Religion.
Sealed in fire under Mary Tudor: Cranmer, Latimer, and Ridley burned at Oxford.
Settled under Elizabeth in the Thirty-Nine Articles; its Puritan fruit bore, in time, the Baptists.
scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
corruption_summary: The age flattens the English Reformation into mere Tudor politics — a king's divorce dressed up as religion — and so misses the gospel God brought through it; others romanticize the medieval church it left and call the recovery a needless rupture.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern secular history tells the English Reformation as nothing but power and appetite: Henry wanted a wife and an heir, dissolved the monasteries for their gold, and religion was the pretext. There is real sin in that telling, and the dictionary does not whitewash Henry. But to stop there is to be blind to what God did: an open Bible in the plowman's tongue, a preached gospel, justification by faith recovered, and martyrs who died not for a king's marriage but for Christ. The Lord is not hindered from working His good through the crooked motives of men.

A second corruption runs the other way — the modern romanticizing of pre-Reformation England as a golden age of faith wickedly torn apart. This forgets the indulgences, the locked-up Scriptures, the gospel buried under merit and Mass. The Reformation was not a rupture of a healthy church but the recovery of a sick one. The principle to keep is that the Word of God, once loosed, cannot be bound (2 Tim 2:9); England's reform stands or falls by that Word, not by the worthiness of the kings who unwittingly served it.
roots_summary: From Latin reformare (to form anew); the English branch of the wider Reformation, rooted in Tyndale's Bible, Cranmer's liturgy, and the Oxford martyrs.
roots_lines: Latin reformare, to form anew, restore to true shape
Tyndale's English New Testament (1526) — the Word in the people's tongue
Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer and the Articles of Religion
The Oxford martyrs — Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley — under Mary Tudor
The Thirty-Nine Articles (1571), settling a Reformed doctrine in England
usage: The English Reformation gave the plowman a Bible he could read and the martyrs a gospel worth burning for.
Latimer's word at the stake — "we shall this day light such a candle" — is the English Reformation in a sentence.
From the unfinished work of the English Reformation the Puritans and then the Baptists pressed on toward a purer church.

etymology: From Marburg, the German town where Philip of Hesse convened the conference in 1529, + colloquy (Latin colloquium, a speaking together); the meeting of Luther and Zwingli over the Lord's Supper.
biblical_def: The Marburg Colloquy of 1529 was the conference at which Philip of Hesse sought to unite the German and Swiss Reformations by reconciling Martin Luther and Huldrych Zwingli. The two streams agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles — the Trinity, the person of Christ, justification by faith, the rejection of the Mass as sacrifice — and broke over the fifteenth: the nature of Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper. Luther held to a bodily presence in, with, and under the bread, chalking on the table the words Hoc est corpus meum, "This is my body," and refusing every figurative reading. Zwingli argued that "is" means "signifies," that Christ's body is at the Father's right hand and cannot be bodily in the bread, and that the Supper is a memorial sign received by faith. At the parting Luther would not grant Zwingli the hand of fellowship, saying they were of a different spirit. The breach was never healed in their lifetimes, and it left the Reformation divided into Lutheran and Reformed. This dictionary, holding the Reformed position, judges Zwingli the nearer to the truth on the letter while owning Calvin's later refinement — a real spiritual feeding on Christ by faith — as the fullest biblical account.
webster_summary: The 1529 conference where Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen articles but split on the Lord's Supper — Luther holding a bodily presence, Zwingli a memorial received by faith. The breach divided the Reformation into Lutheran and Reformed.
webster_full: MARBURG COLLOQUY, noun. The 1529 conference at Marburg, convened by Philip of Hesse, between Luther and Zwingli.
Agreement was reached on fourteen of fifteen articles of doctrine.
The split came on the fifteenth: the manner of Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper.
Luther insisted on a bodily presence ("This is my body"); Zwingli on a memorial sign received by faith.
The breach was not healed; it divided the Reformation into Lutheran and Reformed streams.
scriptures: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things.
The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
corruption_summary: The modern temptation is to call the Marburg breach a sad squabble over words and to wish the Reformers had simply agreed to differ — as though the real presence of Christ in His own ordinance were a matter of indifference rather than of truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecumenical readers treat Marburg as a cautionary tale of stubbornness: if only Luther had unbent, the Protestant house would not have divided. But the question was not trivial. Whether Christ's true body is locally present in the bread touches His humanity, His ascension, and the meaning of His own words. Luther rightly refused to let "is my body" be emptied of all force; Zwingli rightly refused a carnal presence that denies Christ's bodily session at the Father's right hand (Acts 3:21). The dictionary will not flatten that into a misunderstanding over semantics.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but it does meet the modern instinct to prize unity above truth. The principle to recover is that doctrine matters even when it costs fellowship, and that the Lord's Supper is no small thing to err in. Calvin's mature teaching — that believers truly feed on the body and blood of Christ spiritually, by the Holy Spirit and through faith, while Christ remains bodily in heaven — is the dictionary's answer to both errors, and the position the 1689 Confession carries.
roots_summary: From Marburg (the town) + Latin colloquium (a speaking together); the 1529 debate over the words of institution, "This is my body."
roots_lines: Marburg — the Hessian town where Philip of Hesse hosted the conference
Latin colloquium, a conference or speaking together
The point of rupture: Hoc est corpus meum, "This is my body" (1 Cor 11:24)
Lutheran reading: bodily presence in, with, and under the bread
Reformed reading: a memorial sign with a true spiritual feeding by faith
usage: At the Marburg Colloquy the Reformation agreed on fourteen articles and divided over one.
Luther chalked "This is my body" on the Marburg table and would not yield the figurative sense.
The Marburg Colloquy left a wound between Lutheran and Reformed that Calvin labored to heal.

etymology: From Westminster, where the Assembly met in the Abbey's Jerusalem Chamber (1643–49), + confession (Latin confiteri, to acknowledge openly); the Reformed creed it produced.
biblical_def: The Westminster Confession of Faith is the confession of faith drawn up by the Westminster Assembly of Divines between 1643 and 1649, the high-water mark of English-speaking Reformed theology. Summoned by the Long Parliament and aided by Scottish commissioners, some hundred and twenty ministers and learned men labored in the Jerusalem Chamber to frame a confession, two catechisms (Larger and Shorter), a Directory for Public Worship, and a Form of Church Government. The Confession opens, unlike the medieval church, not with the church or the sacraments but with Holy Scripture — its sufficiency, authority, and clarity — and proceeds through the decree of God, creation, providence, the fall, the covenant of grace, Christ the Mediator, effectual calling, justification, adoption, sanctification, and the perseverance of the saints, to the last judgment. Its theology is thoroughly Calvinistic and covenantal. The Shorter Catechism's first question — man's chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy Him forever — has catechized generations. This dictionary's own confession, the 1689 London Baptist Confession, deliberately followed Westminster nearly word for word, departing only on baptism, the church, and the civil magistrate. To honor Westminster is to honor the parent of the Baptist standard.
webster_summary: The Reformed confession produced by the Westminster Assembly (1643–49), with its Larger and Shorter Catechisms — the high point of English-speaking Calvinism, beginning with Scripture and ordered by covenant. The 1689 Baptist Confession follows it closely, parting only on baptism and polity.
webster_full: WESTMINSTER CONFESSION OF FAITH, noun. The confession framed by the Westminster Assembly of Divines, 1643–1649.
Accompanied by the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, a Directory for Worship, and a Form of Church Government.
Thoroughly Calvinistic and covenantal; it opens with the authority and sufficiency of Holy Scripture.
The Shorter Catechism teaches that man's chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy Him forever.
Closely followed by the 1689 London Baptist Confession, which departs on baptism, church, and magistrate.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness.
ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
corruption_summary: The modern church treats confessions as dusty relics or as chains on the conscience, prizing a vague "no creed but Christ" that in practice leaves every man his own pope; others revise the Confession to soften its hard doctrines of election and eternal punishment until it no longer says what its authors meant.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is anti-confessionalism: the claim that a written confession competes with the Bible. But a confession does not stand over Scripture; it stands under it, openly declaring what the church believes the Scripture teaches, so that error has no place to hide. "No creed but the Bible" sounds humble and is often a cover for doctrinal drift, since every heretic also claims the Bible. The Westminster divines bound their confession explicitly to the Word as its only infallible rule.

The second corruption is revision that guts the substance: bodies that keep the name "Westminster" while striking out unconditional election, particular redemption, or eternal conscious punishment, and reading inclusive and affirming doctrine back into a document that knows nothing of it. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the original text, which is fixed and public; the corruption is in the churches that subscribe it with crossed fingers. The principle to recover is honest subscription — to confess what the words mean, or to stop calling oneself by them.
roots_summary: From the Westminster Assembly (1643–49) + Latin confiteri (to acknowledge openly); a covenantal, Calvinistic confession ordered from Scripture to the last judgment.
roots_lines: Westminster — the Assembly met in the Jerusalem Chamber of the Abbey
Latin confiteri, to acknowledge or confess openly
Opens with Holy Scripture — its authority, sufficiency, and clarity
Covenantal structure: the covenant of works and the covenant of grace
Parent text of the 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith
usage: The Westminster Confession of Faith opens not with the church but with the Word of God.
Generations learned that man's chief end is to glorify God from the Westminster Shorter Catechism.
The 1689 Baptist Confession copied the Westminster Confession of Faith almost verbatim, parting on baptism.

etymology: From Latin Helvetia (Switzerland) + confession; the second of the great Swiss Reformed confessions, written by Heinrich Bullinger in 1561 and published in 1566.
biblical_def: The Second Helvetic Confession is the mature confession of the Swiss Reformed churches, composed privately by Heinrich Bullinger — Zwingli's successor at Zurich — in 1561 as his own testimony of faith, and published in 1566 when Elector Frederick III of the Palatinate, under attack for his Reformed convictions, sought a clear statement to defend himself before the imperial diet. It was at once received across the Reformed world: Switzerland, the Palatinate, Scotland, Hungary, Poland, France. Of all the Reformation confessions it had the widest reception. Its thirty chapters open with Scripture as the true Word of God and the rule of faith, declare the preaching of that Word to be the Word of God, and move through the Trinity, providence, predestination, the fall, free will's bondage, justification by faith, the church, the sacraments, and the Christian magistrate. Its tone is warm and pastoral as well as precise, framing doctrine for the comfort and order of the church. This dictionary honors it as one of the chief Reformed standards, kin to the Heidelberg Catechism with which it was so often bound, and as a faithful witness to the sovereign grace the 1689 Confession also professes.
webster_summary: The mature Swiss Reformed confession, written by Heinrich Bullinger in 1561 and published in 1566; the most widely received of the Reformation confessions, opening with Scripture and the preaching of the Word, and confessing the Trinity, predestination, and justification by faith.
webster_full: SECOND HELVETIC CONFESSION, noun. The confession of the Swiss Reformed churches, written by Heinrich Bullinger (1561), published 1566.
The most widely received Reformation confession — adopted in Switzerland, the Palatinate, Scotland, Hungary, Poland, and beyond.
Thirty chapters opening with Holy Scripture as the Word of God and rule of faith.
Declares the preached Word of God to be the Word of God to the hearer.
Confesses the Trinity, predestination, justification by faith, and the Christian magistrate.
scriptures: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
corruption_summary: This confession faces little redefinition, being a settled historic text; the live danger is forgetting it altogether — a Reformed world that prizes novelty and neglects the rich witness of its own confessions, leaving its people unanchored against the doctrines of the age.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the Second Helvetic Confession is corrupted today is chiefly by neglect. Many who name themselves Reformed have never read it, and a church ignorant of its confessions is easy prey for every wind of doctrine (Eph 4:14). Bullinger's clear word that the preached Scripture is the very Word of God rebukes a generation that has traded preaching for performance and the Bible for the felt needs of the hour.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; its text is fixed and public. The principle to recover is the confession's own opening conviction: that Holy Scripture is the true Word of God, sufficient and authoritative, and that faith comes by the hearing of that Word (Rom 10:17). The widest-received confession of the Reformation calls the church back to the Book it was written to defend.
roots_summary: From Latin Helvetia (Switzerland) + confession; Bullinger's 1561 personal testimony, published 1566 as the Swiss Reformed standard and the most widely adopted of the Reformation confessions.
roots_lines: Latin Helvetia, the old name for Switzerland
Written by Heinrich Bullinger, Zwingli's successor at Zurich, in 1561
Published 1566 to defend Frederick III's Reformed faith
Thirty chapters, opening with Scripture as the Word of God
The most widely received of all the Reformation confessions
usage: The Second Helvetic Confession was received from Scotland to Hungary, the most widely adopted of the Reformation creeds.
Bullinger's Second Helvetic Confession teaches that the preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God.
Bound with the Heidelberg Catechism, the Second Helvetic Confession shaped the Reformed churches of Europe.

etymology: Latin consensus (agreement) + Tigurinus (of Zurich, Latin Tigurum); the 1549 agreement on the Lord's Supper between Calvin and Bullinger that united the Swiss Reformed.
biblical_def: The Consensus Tigurinus, the Zurich Agreement of 1549, is the accord on the Lord's Supper hammered out between John Calvin of Geneva and Heinrich Bullinger of Zurich, which united the two streams of the Swiss Reformation into one Reformed church. Where Marburg had failed to reconcile Luther and Zwingli twenty years before, Calvin and Bullinger succeeded among themselves, finding a common confession of the sacrament. They agreed that the bread and wine are signs that truly exhibit what they signify; that Christ is not bodily enclosed in the elements but remains in heaven at the Father's right hand; that the believer, by the secret power of the Holy Spirit and through faith, is truly made partaker of the body and blood of Christ; and that the unbelieving receive only the bare signs to their judgment, not Christ Himself. This struck the via media between a Lutheran corporeal presence and a bare Zwinglian memorialism that emptied the Supper of grace. The Consensus became the seed of the Reformed sacramental doctrine carried into the Heidelberg Catechism, the Belgic Confession, and at last the Westminster and 1689 standards. This dictionary confesses its substance: a real spiritual feeding on Christ, by the Spirit, through faith.
webster_summary: The 1549 Zurich Agreement between Calvin and Bullinger on the Lord's Supper, uniting the Swiss Reformed: the elements are signs that exhibit what they signify, Christ remains in heaven, and believers truly partake of His body and blood by the Spirit through faith.
webster_full: CONSENSUS TIGURINUS, noun. The Zurich Agreement of 1549 on the Lord's Supper between Calvin and Bullinger.
It united the Genevan and Zurich streams into one Reformed church.
The elements are signs that truly exhibit what they signify; Christ remains bodily in heaven.
The believer partakes of Christ's body and blood by the secret power of the Holy Spirit, through faith.
It struck the path between Lutheran corporeal presence and bare Zwinglian memorialism.
scriptures: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.
If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.
For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body.
corruption_summary: The modern Reformed church has too often slid into the very bare memorialism the Consensus resisted — treating the Supper as a mere remembrance with no grace conveyed — while others abandon the Reformed mean for a quasi-Roman or Lutheran corporeal presence.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift in much modern evangelicalism is toward a flattened Zwinglianism: the Lord's Supper is reduced to a memory exercise, a moment of private reflection, with nothing actually given and nothing actually received. The Consensus Tigurinus and the whole Reformed tradition resist this. The sacrament is no empty sign; the Spirit makes the believing communicant a true partaker of Christ's body and blood (1 Cor 10:16). To lose this is to lose the comfort the ordinance was given to convey.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; its danger is forgetfulness, not redefinition. The principle to recover is the Reformed doctrine itself: Christ is bodily in heaven (Col 3:1), yet truly fed upon by faith through the Spirit at His table. The Consensus of Zurich is the historic charter of that doctrine, and it calls the church both away from a carnal presence and back toward a real, Spirit-wrought communion.
roots_summary: From Latin consensus (agreement) + Tigurinus (of Zurich); the 1549 Calvin–Bullinger accord on the Supper, the seed of the Reformed sacramental tradition.
roots_lines: Latin consensus, agreement, common consent
Tigurinus, of Zurich (Latin Tigurum)
The 1549 accord between John Calvin and Heinrich Bullinger
Doctrine: signs that exhibit Christ, fed upon by the Spirit through faith
Seed of the Heidelberg, Belgic, Westminster, and 1689 sacramental teaching
usage: The Consensus Tigurinus did for the Swiss what Marburg had failed to do for Luther and Zwingli.
By the Consensus Tigurinus, Geneva and Zurich confessed one doctrine of the Lord's Supper.
The Reformed mean — Christ in heaven, fed upon by faith — is fixed in the Consensus Tigurinus.

etymology: From synod (Greek synodos, an assembly) + Dort (Dordrecht, the Dutch city); the international Reformed assembly of 1618–19 that condemned Arminianism.
biblical_def: The Synod of Dort (Dordrecht), held in the Dutch Republic from 1618 to 1619, was the great international assembly of Reformed churches summoned to judge the doctrines of the Remonstrants, the followers of Jacobus Arminius. Arminius and his party had raised five articles against the received Reformed teaching, asserting election conditioned on foreseen faith, a universal atonement, resistible grace, and the possibility that the regenerate might finally fall away. Delegates gathered not only from the Netherlands but from England, the Palatinate, Switzerland, Bremen, Hesse, and elsewhere — the most truly ecumenical Reformed council ever held. The Synod weighed the Remonstrance and rejected it, setting forth in answer the Canons of Dort under five heads, which the church has since remembered by the acrostic of the doctrines of grace: total depravity, unconditional election, limited (particular) atonement, irresistible grace, and the perseverance of the saints. These five points are not the whole of Reformed theology but its answer to Arminius at the points he denied. This dictionary confesses the Canons of Dort as a faithful summary of the Scripture's teaching on sovereign saving grace.
webster_summary: The international Reformed assembly of 1618–19 at Dordrecht that judged and rejected the five articles of the Arminian Remonstrants, answering them in the Canons of Dort — the doctrines of grace later remembered as total depravity, unconditional election, particular atonement, irresistible grace, and perseverance.
webster_full: SYNOD OF DORT, noun. The international Reformed synod held at Dordrecht, 1618–1619.
Summoned to judge the five articles of the Arminian Remonstrants.
Delegates came from the Netherlands, England, the Palatinate, Switzerland, and more — the most ecumenical Reformed council.
It rejected the Remonstrance and issued the Canons of Dort under five heads of doctrine.
Those five heads are remembered as the doctrines of sovereign grace.
scriptures: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
corruption_summary: The age recoils from Dort's doctrine as harsh and calls election unfair, preferring an Arminian gospel where the decisive choice is man's; others caricature the five points as the sum of the faith, forgetting they are an answer to a particular error, not a whole theology.
corruption_paragraphs: The deepest corruption Dort confronted, and which never dies, is the Arminian instinct of the natural heart: that grace must wait on the free choice of man, that the sinner is the decisive cause of his own salvation. Scripture answers that salvation is not of him that willeth but of God that sheweth mercy (Rom 9:16), that the Father gives a people to the Son who shall surely come (John 6:37), and that He keeps them so that none is plucked from His hand (John 10:28). Dort did not invent these doctrines; it confessed them against those who denied them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of its history. But a second corruption comes from friends: reducing all of Reformed faith to "five points," as though TULIP were a complete theology rather than a response to the Remonstrants at the five points they disputed. The principle to keep is balance — the doctrines of grace are precious and true, and they sit within the whole counsel of God: the Trinity, covenant, the means of grace, the Christian life, and the glory of God in all.
roots_summary: From Greek synodos (assembly) + Dordrecht; the 1618–19 council that answered Arminianism with the Canons of Dort, the doctrines of sovereign grace.
roots_lines: Greek synodos, a coming together, an assembly
Held at Dordrecht (Dort) in the Dutch Republic, 1618–1619
Convened to judge the five articles of the Arminian Remonstrants
Answered them in the Canons of Dort under five heads of doctrine
The doctrines of grace: depravity, election, particular atonement, grace, perseverance
usage: The Synod of Dort answered Arminius's five articles with the five Canons of grace.
Reformed churches from England to Switzerland sent delegates to the Synod of Dort.
The doctrines remembered as TULIP take their shape from the Canons of the Synod of Dort.

etymology: From Dutch (of the Netherlands) + Reformed; the Calvinist churches of the Low Countries, confessing the Three Forms of Unity.
biblical_def: Dutch Reformed names the Calvinist churches of the Netherlands and their tradition, which grew up amid the eighty-year struggle for liberty against Catholic Spain and became one of the strongest pillars of Reformed Christianity. Their confessional standard is the Three Forms of Unity: the Belgic Confession (1561), written by Guido de Brès, who sealed it with martyrdom; the Heidelberg Catechism (1563), with its tender opening — that a believer's only comfort in life and death is that he is not his own but belongs to his faithful Savior Jesus Christ; and the Canons of Dort (1619), answering the Arminian Remonstrance. From this soil came a flourishing of Reformed life: the precise theology of the Dutch scholastics, the warm experiential piety of the Nadere Reformatie (the "Further Reformation"), and later Abraham Kuyper's vision of Christ's lordship over every sphere of life, with his famous cry that there is not one square inch of all creation over which Christ does not declare "Mine." The tradition carried to America in the Reformed and Christian Reformed churches. This dictionary honors the Dutch Reformed as faithful Calvinist kin, sharing its doctrines of grace while differing, as a Baptist confession must, on the subjects and mode of baptism.
webster_summary: The Calvinist churches of the Netherlands, confessing the Three Forms of Unity — the Belgic Confession, the Heidelberg Catechism, and the Canons of Dort. The tradition of de Brès, the Further Reformation, and Kuyper's lordship-of-Christ-over-all vision.
webster_full: DUTCH REFORMED, adjective / noun. The Calvinist churches of the Netherlands and their tradition.
Confessional standard: the Three Forms of Unity — Belgic Confession, Heidelberg Catechism, Canons of Dort.
Born amid the eighty-year war for liberty against Catholic Spain.
Fruitful in Dutch scholastic theology and the warm piety of the Nadere Reformatie.
Shaped later by Abraham Kuyper's teaching of Christ's lordship over every sphere.
scriptures: The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's.
corruption_summary: Like every once-living Reformed body, the Dutch churches show the marks of decline where the Word was let go — the larger national church long since secularized and the doctrine of the Three Forms confessed by a shrinking remnant; Kuyper's lordship-of-Christ vision is sometimes bent into a mere cultural activism that forgets the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: The historic corruption the Dutch Reformed resisted was Rome's tyranny, sealed in the blood of martyrs like de Brès. The modern corruption is internal decay: the large national church of the Netherlands has, in much of its body, gone the way of European liberalism, while the confessing strength survives in smaller faithful denominations. A church may keep the name "Reformed" long after it has buried the gospel.

A second, subtler corruption distorts Kuyper's good doctrine of Christ's lordship over every sphere into a worldly activism — cultural transformation pursued as though the kingdom came by political effort and not by the preaching of the cross and the new birth. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of its confessional texts. The principle to recover is that Christ's claim on every square inch (Psa 24:1; Col 1:18) begins at the empty tomb and the regenerate heart, not at the ballot box; the Dutch Reformed tradition at its best held both.
roots_summary: From the Netherlands + Reformed; the Calvinist churches confessing the Three Forms of Unity, born in the war against Spain and flowering in the Further Reformation and Kuyper.

The Heidelberg Catechism gave the Dutch Reformed their tender confession of belonging to Christ.

etymology: From Greek ana (again) + baptizein (to baptize); "re-baptizers," the name given by their enemies to the radical Reformers who rejected infant baptism and baptized believers.
biblical_def: The Anabaptists ("re-baptizers") were the radical wing of the sixteenth-century Reformation who, going further than Luther and Zwingli, rejected infant baptism and baptized professing believers — for which their enemies, both Catholic and Protestant, drowned, burned, and beheaded them in great numbers. The movement began in Zurich in 1525 when Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz, dissatisfied with Zwingli's caution, baptized one another on confession of faith; Manz was soon drowned in the Limmat. The Schleitheim Confession of 1527 gave the gentler stream its order. The Anabaptists were not one body but many: the peaceful and biblical, like the Swiss Brethren and the followers of Menno Simons (whence the Mennonites), and the wild and heretical, like the Münster fanatics of 1534–35, who seized a city, practiced polygamy, and brought lasting disgrace on the name. This dictionary distinguishes sharply. It owns the recovery of believer's baptism and the gathered church of the regenerate as biblical truths the magisterial Reformers left unfinished — truths the later Baptists carried — while rejecting the Münster excesses, the pacifist denial of the magistrate's sword, and the soul-sleep and other errors that marred parts of the movement.
webster_summary: The radical Reformers who rejected infant baptism and baptized believers, suffering fierce persecution from Catholic and Protestant alike. A mixed movement — the biblical Swiss Brethren and Mennonites alongside the Münster fanatics. This dictionary owns their recovery of believer's baptism while rejecting their excesses and errors.
webster_full: ANABAPTISTS, noun. The radical Reformers (so named "re-baptizers") who rejected infant baptism and baptized professing believers.
Begun at Zurich in 1525 with Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz; Manz was soon drowned for it.
The Schleitheim Confession (1527) ordered the peaceful Swiss Brethren stream.
A mixed movement: the biblical Mennonites (Menno Simons) and the heretical Münster fanatics (1534–35).
This dictionary owns their recovery of believer's baptism, rejecting the Münster errors and pacifist denial of the magistrate.
scriptures: Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.
He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.
for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
corruption_summary: The name "Anabaptist" is corrupted in two ways: by the Münster fanatics who disgraced it with violence and polygamy, and by modern writers who flatten all Anabaptists into a single pacifist, anti-creedal, proto-progressive movement and claim them as forerunners of a doctrine-light Christianity they would not have recognized.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is historical: the Münster rebellion of 1534–35, where men calling themselves Anabaptists seized a city, declared a new Jerusalem, practiced polygamy, and were crushed in blood. Their enemies used Münster forever after to slander every believer who held believer's baptism. The dictionary names the Münster men as fanatics and heretics, and distinguishes them from the godly Swiss Brethren and Mennonites who suffered for a biblical conviction.

The second corruption is modern: the romantic claiming of the Anabaptists as forerunners of a creedless, pacifist, socially-progressive Christianity over against the "rigid" confessional Reformers. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the documented history, but it does face this selective reading. The Baptists who carried forward believer's baptism were confessional men (the 1644 and 1689 Confessions), not anti-doctrinal; they held the magistrate's God-given sword (Rom 13:4) against the pacifist wing. The principle to recover is that believer's baptism is a biblical recovery (Acts 2:41; 8:37), to be received with the whole counsel of God, not as a banner for whatever the age wishes the Anabaptists had been.
roots_summary: From Greek ana (again) + baptizein (to baptize) — "re-baptizers," a name of scorn for those who baptized believers, rejecting infant baptism.

etymology: From Reformed + scholasticism (Latin schola, school); the rigorous school-method theology of the Reformed orthodox in the seventeenth century.
biblical_def: Reformed Scholasticism names the precise, school-method theology of the Reformed orthodox in the age after the first Reformers — roughly from the late sixteenth century through the seventeenth — when men like Francis Turretin, Gisbertus Voetius, Johann Heinrich Heidegger, and the framers of the great confessions set the recovered gospel in careful, ordered, defensible form. The first Reformers had preached and disputed; their heirs had to teach the faith in the universities, defend it against able Catholic and Arminian and Socinian opponents, and hand it on whole to the next generation. So they took up the rigorous tools of definition, distinction, and disputation — the old scholastic method — and filled them with Reformation content. Turretin's Institutes of Elenctic Theology is the towering monument, examining each doctrine by stating the question, drawing the necessary distinctions, and answering objections. This was not, as later caricature would have it, a cold rationalism that betrayed Calvin's warmth; it was the careful guarding of a precious deposit. This dictionary honors the Reformed scholastics as the architects of confessional precision, and owns that the 1689 Baptist Confession itself is a fruit of their ordered, biblical, God-glorifying labor.
webster_summary: The precise, school-method theology of the seventeenth-century Reformed orthodox — Turretin, Voetius, and the confessional framers — who set the recovered gospel in careful, ordered, defensible form against able opponents. Not a cold rationalism but the guarding of a precious deposit.
webster_full: REFORMED SCHOLASTICISM, noun. The rigorous school-method theology of the Reformed orthodox, c. 1565–1725.
Practiced by Francis Turretin, Gisbertus Voetius, Heidegger, and the confessional framers.
It took up the scholastic tools of definition, distinction, and disputation, filled with Reformation content.
Turretin's Institutes of Elenctic Theology is its towering monument.
Not a betrayal of Calvin's warmth but the careful guarding of the gospel deposit.
scriptures: That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called.
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
corruption_summary: The modern caricature pits a warm-hearted Calvin against a cold, rationalistic scholastic orthodoxy that supposedly buried the gospel under hair-splitting logic — a slander corrected by recent careful study, but still repeated to excuse a doctrine-light, anti-precision piety.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is the "Calvin against the Calvinists" thesis: the claim that the warm, biblical Calvin was betrayed by his rigid scholastic heirs, who replaced living faith with logical systems and a central dogma of predestination ground out by reason. Sober study of the sources has refuted this caricature; the Reformed orthodox were exegetes and pastors as well as logicians, and their precision served the gospel, not a system. The dictionary rejects the slander.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but the caricature is often pressed into service to justify a doctrine-averse spirit — as if careful definition were itself unspiritual. Scripture commands the opposite: keep the deposit (2 Tim 1:14), hold fast the faithful word and convince the gainsayers (Titus 1:9), rightly divide the word of truth (2 Tim 2:15). The principle to recover is that precision is a form of love — the Reformed scholastics labored at definitions so that the church would not lose the gospel to able and subtle error.
roots_summary: From Reformed + Latin schola (school); the careful, ordered, disputational theology of the Reformed orthodox, guarding the Reformation gospel in confessional precision.
